claims.text: Elemental Cr coatings on zirconium-alloy cladding experience interdiffusion-related degradation at elevated temperatures.
CrAl is a candidate metallic protective coating for zirconium-alloy cladding.
Adding a few atomic percent Al to an elemental Cr coating is an appropriate way to create the proposed Cr-Al coating.
Al addition will cause in-situ formation of Al2O3 at the Cr/Zr interface.
The interfacial Al2O3 layer will be dense and continuous.
Al2O3 will also form within the Cr-Al coating microstructure.
The resulting alumina will act as a diffusion barrier.
Al in the Cr-Al coating will oxidize preferentially.
The alumina barrier will inhibit mutual diffusion of Cr and Zr across the coating-substrate interface.
Inhibiting Cr-Zr interdiffusion will preserve coating integrity during prolonged exposure to subcritical water and high-temperature steam.
The proposed coating is intended for PWR primary water and accident-relevant high-temperature steam.
The applicable temperature boundaries are approximately 300°C for normal PWR operation and 800–1200°C for accident steam exposure.
Relative to elemental Cr, the Cr-Al coating will exhibit slower Cr-Zr interdiffusion.
Relative to elemental Cr, the Cr-Al coating will exhibit less oxidation-related degradation in both PWR water and high-temperature steam.
Relative to elemental Cr, the Cr-Al coating will have improved mechanical stability in both service regimes.
The optimal Al content and long-term behavior under neutron irradiation remain uncertain.
The proposed experiment directly compares Al-doped and unmodified Cr coatings under both simulated PWR-water and high-temperature-steam exposures.
Depth profiling, oxidation weight gain, and adhesion plus microscopy measurements separately evaluate interdiffusion, oxidation behavior, and coating integrity.
Failure to obtain statistically significant improvements in interdiffusion, oxidation resistance, and mechanical stability under both environments would falsify the hypothesis.
